jobs.subject: Happy New Month — a little reminder for your parenting journey
jobs.bodyText:
Happy New Month 💜

We’ve stepped into a new month — and a new quarter.

Before the year runs away with us, this may be a good time to pause and reflect on your parenting journey so far.

What has gone well?
What has felt hard?
What have you been learning about yourself, your children and your family?
What would you like to be more intentional about in the months ahead?

And if you have reached a point where you are thinking, “God has to help me with this,” I understand.

Because I can’t even lie — parenting is very spiritual. We need God’s wisdom, strength, help and grace.

In case you didn’t know, at Lit Lambs we pray together every first Saturday of the month at 6:00 AM WAT. It is simply a time to seek God intentionally about our parenting journey, our children and our families.

This Saturday, October 3, we’ll be praying again.

If you’d like to join us, use the link below to join the WhatsApp group. The prayer details will be shared there:

https://chat.whatsapp.com/IXpA5Q0IHx25cUTyqqoxjs?s=cl&p=i&mlu=4&ilr=4

Happy New Month. I pray October brings you fresh grace, wisdom and strength for your family.

Lesi
Founder, Lit Lambs

jobs.subject: What does your child hear when someone gets it wrong?
jobs.bodyText:
Have you ever been really upset about something someone did and talked about it in front of your children?

“She’s so irresponsible.”

“He’s selfish.”

“That’s just the way she is.”

Maybe what the person did was genuinely wrong, and you felt frustrated or hurt.

But there’s something I need us to pay attention to as parents.

Our children do not only learn from what we say to them. They also learn from how we talk about other people, especially when those people do something wrong.

When a child repeatedly hears us label a whole person because of something they did, they could begin to connect the wrong action to the person’s identity.

She acted irresponsibly, so she is irresponsible.

And that same thinking could become:

I failed, so I am a failure.

I did something bad, so I am bad.

I acted irresponsibly, so I am irresponsible.

And I’m not sure that is what we want.

We want children who know who they are and can make mistakes without taking on the label of their mistakes.

So while we are intentional about affirming their identity, let’s also pay attention to what we may be teaching indirectly through the way we talk about other people.

Lesi
Founder, Lit Lambs
